   126	## Features
   127	
   128	* Import meshes from binary/ASCII STL, Wavefront OBJ, ASCII OFF, binary/ASCII PLY, GLTF/GLB 2.0, 3MF, XAML, 3DXML, etc.
   129	* Import and export 2D or 3D vector paths from/to DXF or SVG files
   130	* Import geometry files using the GMSH SDK if installed (BREP, STEP, IGES, INP, BDF, etc)
   131	* Export meshes as binary STL, binary PLY, ASCII OFF, OBJ, GLTF/GLB 2.0, COLLADA, etc.
   132	* Export meshes using the GMSH SDK if installed (Abaqus INP, Nastran BDF, etc)
   133	* Preview meshes using pyglet or in- line in jupyter notebooks using three.js
   134	* Automatic hashing of numpy arrays for change tracking using MD5, zlib CRC, or xxhash
   135	* Internal caching of computed values validated from hashes
   136	* Calculate face adjacencies, face angles, vertex defects, etc.
   137	* Calculate cross sections, i.e. the slicing operation used in 3D printing
   138	* Slice meshes with one or multiple arbitrary planes and return the resulting surface
   139	* Split mesh based on face connectivity using networkx, graph-tool, or scipy.sparse
   140	* Calculate mass properties, including volume, center of mass, moment of inertia, principal components of inertia vectors and components
   141	* Repair simple problems with triangle winding, normals, and quad/tri holes
   142	* Convex hulls of meshes
   143	* Compute rotation/translation/tessellation invariant identifier and find duplicate meshes
   144	* Determine if a mesh is watertight, convex, etc.
   145	* Uniformly sample the surface of a mesh
   146	* Ray-mesh queries including location, triangle index, etc.
   147	* Boolean operations on meshes (intersection, union, difference) using OpenSCAD or Blender as a back end. Note that mesh booleans in general are usually slow and unreliable
   148	* Voxelize watertight meshes
   149	* Volume mesh generation (TETgen) using Gmsh SDK
   150	* Smooth watertight meshes using laplacian smoothing algorithms (Classic, Taubin, Humphrey)
   151	* Subdivide faces of a mesh
   152	* Minimum volume oriented bounding boxes for meshes
   153	* Minimum volume bounding spheres
   154	* Symbolic integration of functions over triangles
   155	* Calculate nearest point on mesh surface and signed distance
   156	* Determine if a point lies inside or outside of a well constructed mesh using signed distance
   157	* Primitive objects (Box, Cylinder, Sphere, Extrusion) which are subclassed Trimesh objects and have all the same features (inertia, viewers, etc)
   158	* Simple scene graph and transform tree which can be rendered (pyglet window, three.js in a jupyter notebook, [pyrender](https://github.com/mmatl/pyrender)) or exported.

   194	## Which Mesh Format Should I Use?
   195	
   196	Quick recommendation: `GLB` or `PLY`. Every time you replace `OBJ` with `GLB` an angel gets its wings.
   197	
   198	If you want things like by-index faces, instancing, colors, textures, etc, `GLB` is a terrific choice. GLTF/GLB is an [extremely well specified](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/master/specification/2.0) modern format that is easy and fast to parse: it has a JSON header describing data in a binary blob. It has a simple hierarchical scene graph, a great looking modern physically based material system, support in [dozens-to-hundreds of libraries](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/issues/1058), and a [John Carmack endorsment](https://www.khronos.org/news/press/significant-gltf-momentum-for-efficient-transmission-of-3d-scenes-models). Note that GLTF is a large specification, and `trimesh` only supports a subset of features: loading basic geometry is supported, NOT supported are fancier things like animations, skeletons, etc.
   199	
   200	In the wild, `STL` is perhaps the most common format. `STL` files are extremely simple: it is basically just a list of triangles. They are robust and are a good choice for basic geometry. Binary `PLY` files are a good step up, as they support indexed faces and colors.
   201	
   202	Wavefront `OBJ` is also pretty common: unfortunately OBJ doesn't have a widely accepted specification so every importer and exporter implements things slightly differently, making it tough to support. It also allows unfortunate things like arbitrary sized polygons, has a face representation which is easy to mess up, references other files for materials and textures, arbitrarily interleaves data, and is slow to parse. Give `GLB` or `PLY` a try as an alternative!

Built on top of [sktime](https://www.sktime.net/en/stable/) and [numpyro](https://num.pyro.ai/en/stable/), Prophetverse aims to provide a flexible and easy-to-use library for time series forecasting with a focus on interpretability and customizability. It is particularly useful for Marketing Mix Modeling, where understanding the effect of different marketing channels on sales is crucial. 14 15 16 17 ## Table of Contents 18 - [🚀 Installation](#-installation) 19 - [📊 Forecasting with default hyperparameters](#-forecasting-with-default-hyperparameters) 20 - [🌟 Features & Comparison with Meta's Prophet](#-features--comparison-with-metas-prophet) 21 - [🤝 Contributing to Prophetverse](#-contributing-to-prophetverse) 22 - [📚 Documentation](#-documentation) 23 - [🗺 Roadmap](https://github.com/felipeangelimvieira/prophetverse/discussions/99) 24 25 ## 🚀 Installation 26 27 To install with pip: 28 29 ```bash 30 pip install prophetverse 31 ``` 32 33 Or with poetry: 34 35 ```bash 36 poetry add prophetverse 37 ``` 38 39 ## 📊 Forecasting with default hyperparameters 40 41 Prophetverse model provides an interface compatible with sktime. Here's how to use it: 42 43 ```python 44 from prophetverse.sktime import Prophetverse 45 46 # Create the model 47 model = Prophetverse() 48 49 # Fit the model 50 model.fit(y=y, X=X) 51 52 # Forecast in sample 53 y_pred = model.predict(X=X, fh=[1,2,3,4]) 54 ``` 55 56 ## 🌟 Features & Comparison with Meta's Prophet 57 58 Prophetverse is similar to the original Prophet model in many aspects, but it has some differences and new features. The following table summarizes the main features of Prophetverse and compares them with the original Prophet model: 59 60 61 62 | Feature | Prophetverse | Original Prophet | Motivation | 63 |---------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------| ----------------------------------------- | 64 | **Logistic trend** | Capacity as a random variable | Capacity as a hyperparameter, user input required | The capacity is usually unknown by the users. Having it as a variable is useful for Total Addressable Market inference | 65 | **Custom trend** | Customizable trend functions | Not available | Users can create custom trends and leverage their knowledge about the timeseries to enhance long-term accuracy | 66 | **Likelihoods** | Gaussian, Gamma and Negative Binomial | Gaussian only | Gaussian likelihood fails to provide good forecasts to positive-only and count data (sales, for example) | 67 | **Custom priors** | Supports custom priors for model parameters and exogenous variables | Not supported | Forcing positive coefficients, using prior knowledge to model the timeseries| 68 | **Custom exogenous effects** | Non-linear and customizable effects for exogenous variables, shared coefficients between time series | Not available | Users can create any kind of relationship between exogenous variables and the timeseries, which can be useful for Marketing Mix Modeling and other applications. | 69 | **Changepoints** | Uses changepoint interval | Uses changepoint number | The changepoint number is not stable in the sense that, when the size of timeseries increases, its impact on forecast changes. Think about setting a changepoint number when timeseries has 6 months, and forecasting in future with 2 years of data (4x time original size). Re-tuning would be required. Prophetverse is expected to be more stable | 70 | **Scaling** | Time series scaled internally, exogenous variables scaled by the user | Time series scaled internally | Scaling `y` is needed to enhance user experience with hyperparameters. On the other hand, not scaling the exogenous variables provide more control to the user and they can leverage sktime's transformers to handle that. | 71 | **Seasonality** | Fourier terms for seasonality passed as exogenous variables | Built-in seasonality handling | Setting up seasonality requires almost zero effort by using `LinearFourierSeasonality` in Prophetverse. The idea is to allow the user to create custom seasonalities easily, without hardcoding it in the code. | 72 | **Multivariate model** | Hierarchical model with multivariate normal likelihood and LKJ prior, bottom-up forecast | Not available | Having shared coefficients, using global information to enhance individual forecast.|| **Inference methods** | MCMC and MAP | MCMC and MAP | | 73 | **Implementation** | Numpyro | Stan 74 75 76 ## 🤝 Contributing to Prophetverse 77 78 We welcome contributions! ### 1.1-1.3 Problem Analysis

The issue describes an inconsistency in matrix computation methods for two quantum operations: **Barrier** and **WireCut**.

**Key Technical Details:**
- **Methods involved**: `qml.matrix(op)` vs `op.matrix()`
- **Error message**: `pennylane.operation.MatrixUndefinedError`
- **Stack trace locations**: `operation.py` lines 1405 and 446
- **Operations affected**: `qml.Barrier(0)` and `qml.WireCut(0)`
- **Expected matrix result**: `array([[1.]])`

**Clear Problem Statement:**
There's inconsistent behavior between the global `qml.matrix()` function and the instance method `.matrix()` for Barrier and WireCut operations. The global function succeeds and returns a 1×1 identity matrix, while the instance method fails with a `MatrixUndefinedError`. Both should behave consistently.

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Import pennylane as qml
2. Create a Barrier operation: `op = qml.Barrier(0)`
3. Call `qml.matrix(op)` → Returns `array([[1.]])` (success)
4. Call `op.matrix()` → Raises `MatrixUndefinedError` (failure)
5. Same behavior occurs with `qml.WireCut(0)`

### 1.5 Best Practices for Testing and Fixing
- Ensure consistency between global and instance methods
- Make minimal changes to preserve existing functionality
- Understand why `qml.matrix()` works differently from `op.matrix()`
- Test both Barrier and WireCut operations

### 1.1-1.3 Problem Analysis

The issue is with **netCDF file reading** when dealing with **grouped files that contain unlimited dimensions**. 

**Technical Details:**
- **File name**: `cm4twc_dump_file.nc`
- **Method**: `cfdm.read()`
- **Class**: `cfdm.read_write.netcdf.NetCDFRead`
- **Error symptom**: Unlimited dimension shows size 0 instead of actual size (13)
- **Field example**: `<Field: transfer_i(time(0), altitude(1), latitude(4), longitude(3)) 1>`

**Problem Explanation:**
When reading grouped netCDF files with unlimited dimensions, the `NetCDFRead` class incorrectly obtains dimension sizes from a flattened version of the file. This flattened representation loses the actual size information for unlimited dimensions because it contains no arrays, causing unlimited dimensions to appear as size 0 instead of their true size.

4. Attempt operations like subspacing on the zero-sized dimension to see downstream errors

### 1.1-1.5 Problem Analysis

**Problem in Clear Terms:**
When cancelling a TaskGroup that contains a task which is in the process of starting another task in a different TaskGroup, the cancellation incorrectly propagates to the destination TaskGroup as well. This violates the expected isolation between TaskGroup scopes.

**Technical Details:**
- Methods: `TaskGroup.start()`, `TaskGroup.start_soon()`, `cancel_scope.cancel()`

    69	## GPX version
    70	
    71	gpx.py can parse and generate GPX 1.0 and 1.1 files. The generated file will always be a valid XML document, but it may not be (strictly speaking) a valid GPX document. For example, if you set gpx.email to "my.email AT mail.com" the generated GPX tag won't confirm to the regex pattern. And the file won't be valid. Most applications will ignore such errors, but... Be aware of this!
    72	
    73	Be aware that the gpxpy object model *is not 100% equivalent* with the underlying GPX XML file schema. That's because the library object model works with both GPX 1.0 and 1.1.
    74	
    75	For example, GPX 1.0 specified a `speed` attribute for every track point, but that was removed in GPX 1.1. If you parse GPX 1.0 and serialize back with `gpx.to_xml()` everything will work fine. But if you have a GPX 1.1 object, changes in the `speed` attribute will be lost after `gpx.to_xml()`. If you want to force using 1.0, you can `gpx.to_xml(version="1.0")`. Another possibility is to use `extensions` to save the speed in GPX 1.1.
    76	
    77	## GPX extensions
    78	
    79	gpx.py preserves GPX extensions. They are stored as [ElementTree](https://docs.python.org/2/library/xml.etree.elementtree.html#module-xml.etree.ElementTree) DOM objects. Extensions are part of GPX 1.1, and will be ignored when serializing a GPX object in a GPX 1.0 file.
    80	
    81	## XML parsing
    82	
    83	If lxml is available, then it will be used for XML parsing, otherwise minidom is used. Lxml is 2-3 times faster so, if you can choose -- use it.
    84	
    85	The GPX version is automatically determined when parsing by reading the version attribute in the gpx node. If this attribute is not present then the version is assumed to be 1.0. A specific version can be forced by setting the `version` parameter in the parse function. Possible values for the 'version' parameter are `1.0`, `1.1` and `None`.
    86	
    87	## GPX max speed
    88	
    89	Gpxpy is a GPX parser and by using it you have access to all the data from the original GPX file. The additional methods to calculate stats have some additional heuristics to remove common GPS errors. For example, to calculate `max_speed` it removes the top `5%` of speeds and points with nonstandard distance (those are usually GPS errors).
    90	
    91	"Raw" max speed can be calculated with:
    92	
    93	    moving_data = gpx.get_moving_data(raw=True)

Bug: deploy with large SAM_CLI_POLL_DELAY has a wrong display (nightly)
### Description:
_Not a breaking bug, more like a display and timing bug_

If we use the feature from my last PR #3500, using `SAM_CLI_POLL_DELAY` with a large delay like a minute, the events retrieved during the poll will be displayed in reverse order (because `describe-stack-events` is in reverse chronological order).

Also during the sleep, the deployment can end and another process could start another deploy so the stack will be `IN_PROGRESS` again and when the first `sam deploy` wakes up it misses the end of the first deployment and will keep running and catch the events of the second deployment.


### Steps to reproduce:
Use [`sam-cli-nightly`](https://github.com/aws/aws-sam-cli/releases/tag/sam-cli-nightly)
`SAM_CLI_POLL_DELAY=60 sam deploy ...`

Check on `cloudformation` that the stack completes and while the first CLI is still running (sleeping)
Run `sam deploy ...` again in another tty.


### Observed result:
Wrong order and display 2 deployments
```
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ResourceStatus                 ResourceType                   LogicalResourceId              ResourceStatusReason
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE_COMPLETE_CLEANUP_IN_P   AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     my-stack                       -
ROGRESS
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS             AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS             AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS             AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS             AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS             AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     my-stack                       User Initiated
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     my-stack                       -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     my-stack                       -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
UPDATE_COMPLETE_CLEANUP_IN_P   AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     my-stack                       -
ROGRESS
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```


### Expected result:

```
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ResourceStatus                 ResourceType                   LogicalResourceId              ResourceStatusReason
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS             AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS             AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
UPDATE_COMPLETE_CLEANUP_IN_P   AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     my-stack                       -
ROGRESS
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     DynamoApp                      -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     AsyncLambdaApp                 -
UPDATE_COMPLETE                AWS::CloudFormation::Stack     my-stack                       -
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```


### Additional environment details (Ex: Windows, Mac, Amazon Linux etc)

`[Unstable] Nightly Release v1.50.0.dev202205260901 - 2022-05-26`

---

### Solution

1: In [`describe_stack_events`](https://github.com/aws/aws-sam-cli/blob/aa75d721b1b463e0a4f2717524cfee80e9fac9d2/samcli/lib/deploy/deployer.py#L364) Instead of immediately print events, they should be buffered during pagination loop and reordered to print.

And in the reordered list find if the stack is not in progress to skip other deployments events (explained in https://github.com/aws/aws-sam-cli/issues/3911).
Maybe we could use `EventId` instead of `Timestamp` to have an exact comparison ?

2: Or maybe we could see with the `cloudformation` team if the [`DescribeStackEvents`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeStackEvents.html) could be improved to pass the order and starting `EventId` or `Timestamp` and it does the ordering/filter for us.
(As the second solution might take some time, I'll go on the first one)

3. Observe "Starting new HTTPS connection" log entries for each request

- Maintain backward compatibility

### 1.1-1.5 Problem Analysis

**Problem Restatement**: Django models using `MachineMixin` behave inconsistently when created in different test setup methods. Models created in `setUpTestData` (runs once per test class) bypass transition conditions, while models created in `setUp` (runs before each test) properly enforce conditions.

**Key Technical Details**:
- **Method names**: `setUpTestData`, `setUp`, `send()`, `let_me_be_visible`
- **Classes**: `MachineMixin`, `StateMachine`, `MyContext`
- **Error**: `TransitionNotAllowed` exception should be raised but isn't for `setUpTestData` instances
- **Files mentioned**: `statemachines.py`, `models.py`, `tests.py`

**Root Cause Hypothesis**: The `MachineMixin` likely caches the state machine instance on the model, and Django's test database isolation causes cached references to become stale or inconsistent when objects are created in `setUpTestData`.

**Reproduction Steps**:
1. Create a Django model with `MachineMixin` and a condition-based transition
2. Set the condition to `False` to block the transition
3. Create model instances in `setUpTestData`
4. Attempt the blocked transition - it incorrectly succeeds
5. Compare with instances created in `setUp` - they correctly block the transition

### 1.1-1.3 Problem Analysis

The issue involves a bug in the `cfdm.read` function (specifically in `cfdm.read_write.netcdf.NetCDFRead`) where:
- **File**: `cm4twc_dump_file.nc` (contains subgroups and has an unlimited dimension)
- **Expected behavior**: Unlimited dimension should show its actual size (13)
- **Actual behavior**: Unlimited dimension shows size 0 when read
- **Root cause**: Dimension sizes are taken from the flattened version of the file, which doesn't preserve unlimited dimension sizes because it contains no arrays
- **Error manifestation**: Downstream operations like subspacing fail due to zero-sized dimensions

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Have a grouped netCDF file with an unlimited dimension of known size
2. Call `cfdm.read('filename.nc')[0]` 
3. Observe that field shows unlimited dimension with size 0 instead of actual size
4. Attempt operations like subspacing on the zero-sized dimension to see downstream errors

### 1.5 Best Practices for Testing and Fixing
- Focus on the NetCDF reading logic in `cfdm.read_write.netcdf.NetCDFRead`
- Ensure dimension size retrieval uses the original grouped file instead of flattened version
- Test with both grouped and regular netCDF files to avoid breaking existing functionality
- Make minimal, targeted changes

<issue_description>
'Canvas.add()' checks boundary but  'Canvas.insert()' doesn't
**Software Versions**
* Python: 3.8.12
* OS: Linux Mint 20.2 Mate Edition
* Kivy: master 714f4935085d4ac0c220fdf7183fb35175f8bcad
* Kivy installation method: `git clone` then `python -m pip install -e ".[dev,full]"`

### Issue

There was a canvas containing a `before` group and an `after` group.

```python
from kivy.uix.widget import Widget

c = Widget().canvas

def print_children(c):
    print([i.__class__.__name__ for i in c.children])

print_children(c)
c.before
c.after
print_children(c)
```

```
[]
['CanvasBase', 'CanvasBase']
```

When  I called `c.insert(0, PushMatrix())` and `c.add(PopMatrix())`, I was expecting the `c.children` to be either of

- `['CanvasBase', 'PushMatrix', 'PopMatrix', 'CanvasBase']` or
- `['PushMatrix', 'CanvasBase', 'CanvasBase', 'PopMatrix']`

but neither was an actual result.

```python
c.insert(0, PushMatrix())
c.add(PopMatrix())
print_children(c)
```

```
['PushMatrix', 'CanvasBase', 'PopMatrix', 'CanvasBase']
```

### Cause

The cause of the issue is that `Canvas` overrides `InstructionGroup.add()` but doesn't  override `InstructionGroup.insert()`.
https://github.com/kivy/kivy/blob/714f4935085d4ac0c220fdf7183fb35175f8bcad/kivy/graphics/instructions.pyx#L656-L662

As you can see, `Canvas.add()` does some check so that the `after` group always remains the last one, which is why I couldn't add a PopMatrix behind the `after` group. https://github.com/kivy/kivy/blob/714f4935085d4ac0c220fdf7183fb35175f8bcad/kivy/graphics/instructions.pyx#L191-L195

### 1.1 Problem Analysis

The issue is about supporting decomposition of multi-controlled RZ gates in PennyLane. Currently, when trying to decompose a controlled RZ gate with multiple control wires, a `DecompositionUndefinedError` is raised.

### 1.2 Technical Details Highlighted

- **Error Message**: `DecompositionUndefinedError`
- **Method Names**: `Controlled.decomposition()`, `_decompose_no_control_values`
- **File Name**: `qml.ops.op_math.controlled.py`
- **Stack Trace Location**: Line 497 in `controlled.py`
- **Classes**: `Controlled` operations
- **Operations**: `qml.RZ`, `qml.PauliX`, `qml.MultiControlledX`

### 1.3 Clear Problem Statement

Multi-controlled RZ gates (created using `qml.ctrl(qml.RZ(...), control=[...])`) cannot be decomposed into elementary operations, unlike multi-controlled PauliX gates. This prevents their use with certain devices and breaks expected functionality.

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a multi-controlled RZ gate: `qml.ctrl(qml.RZ(0, wires=[0]), control=[1,2])`
2. Try to get its decomposition: `.decomposition()`
3. Observe the `DecompositionUndefinedError`

- Follow existing patterns in the codebase for similar decompositions
- Ensure the decomposition is mathematically equivalent to the original operation
- Test with various numbers of control wires
- Verify compatibility with plugin devices
- Maintain consistency with existing controlled operation implementations

<issue_description>
Converting trailing commas to leading causes unexpected indentation in specific cases
### Search before asking

- [X] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

In some cases where SQLFluff is fixing/linting trailing commas to be leading commas within a SELECT statement, the following elements are indented forward for reasons unknown. 

Specifically, this seems to occur when a trailing comma immediately follows an aliased element, and then that element is followed by an empty blank line. For example:

```
SELECT
    acct_id,
    date_x,
    't' AS test,

    CASE
        WHEN condition_1 = '1' THEN ''
        ELSE condition_1
    END AS case_1,

    CASE
        WHEN condition_2 = '2' THEN ''
        ELSE condition_2
    END AS case_2,

    CASE
        WHEN condition_3 = '3' THEN ''
        ELSE condition_3
    END AS case_3,

    closing_date as cls_dt,
    CASE
        WHEN condition_4 = '4' THEN ''
        ELSE condition_4
    END AS case_4,
    dollar_amt,
FROM
    table_x
```

In this example, `'t' AS test,` is followed by an empty line, and then a `CASE` statement. 

### Expected Behaviour

I would expect the configured package to transform the above query into:

```
SELECT
    acct_id
    , date_x
    , 't' AS test

    , CASE
        WHEN condition_1 = '1' THEN ''
        ELSE condition_1
    END AS case_1

    , CASE
        WHEN condition_2 = '2' THEN ''
        ELSE condition_2
    END AS case_2

    , CASE
        WHEN condition_3 = '3' THEN ''
        ELSE condition_3
    END AS case_3

    , closing_date AS cls_dt
    , CASE
        WHEN condition_4 = '4' THEN ''
        ELSE condition_4
    END AS case_4
    , dollar_amt
FROM
    table_x

```

Nothing has changed, except for the commas becoming leading instead of trailing.

                    WHEN condition_3 = '3' THEN ''
                    ELSE condition_3

                    AS case_3

                    , CASE
                        WHEN condition_4 = '4' THEN ''
                        ELSE condition_4

Cycle flow error with apply_map
Hi:

## Description
Using `apply_map`with multiple variables returns cyclical graph.  The `apply_map` function adds a "**random**" dependency from a downstream task to an upstream task.

For more context see [slack thread](https://prefect-community.slack.com/archives/CL09KU1K7/p1607732581070700)

## Reproduction
```
from prefect import Flow, task, case, apply_map, Parameter, unmapped
from prefect.tasks.control_flow import merge

@task
def generate_input1():
    return{
        "num":1,
        "text": "hello"
    }
@task
def generate_input2():
    return {
        "num":2,
        "text": "bye"
    }


@task
def inc(input1, squared):
    return (input1["num"] + 1)**squared

@task
def negate(input1, input2):
    return input1.extend(input2)

@task
def is_even(input1):
    return input1["num"] % 2 == 0

def inc_or_negate(input1, input2, squared):
    
    cond = is_even(input1)

    # If x is even, increment it
    with case(cond, True):
        res1 = inc(input1, unmapped(squared))

    # If x is odd, negate it
    with case(cond, False):
        res2 = negate(input1, input2)
    
    return merge(res1, res2)

with Flow("apply-map example") as flow:
    
    squared = Parameter("squared", default=2)

    input1 = generate_input1.map()
    input2 = generate_input2.map()
    
    result = apply_map(inc_or_negate, input1, input2, squared)


flow.visualize()

state = flow.run()

flow.visualize(flow_state=state)
```

- **File mentioned:** `core/dbt/dataclass_schemas.py`, method `dbtClassMixin.json_schema`

**Steps to Reproduce:**
1. Create a dataclass (e.g., `WritableManifest`)
2. Generate JSON schema using `build_json_schema(all_refs=True)`
3. Attempt to validate data against the generated schema
4. Observe `RefResolutionError` because root schema is a reference

**Best Practices for Fix:**
- Root schema object should remain concrete, not become a reference
- Nested objects can still be referenced for size optimization
- Maintain backward compatibility
- Follow JSON Schema specification requirements

The issue is with **Zope's security proxy** not properly mimicking Python's standard behavior for `str()` and `__repr__()` methods.

- **Expected behavior**: `str(obj)` should equal `repr(obj)` when `obj` has `__repr__()` but no `__str__()`
- **Actual behavior**: `str(proxy)` returns generic proxy string instead of falling back to `__repr__()`

The issue describes a performance problem in PyRollbar's locals() logging functionality:

**Key Technical Details:**
- **File affected**: `traverse.py`
- **Problematic code pattern**: `list(traverse(elem, key=key + (i,), **kw) for i, elem in enumerate(obj))`

- **Method names**: `list_handler`, `traverse`, `enumerate`
- **Variables**: `obj`, `key`, `elem`, `i`

**Clear Problem Statement:**
The current implementation traverses entire large data structures (lists, dictionaries with 100k+ objects) completely before applying size limits. This causes excessive memory usage and processing time in a logging library, which should have bounded resource consumption. Additionally, there's no recursion depth limit, allowing deeply nested or degenerate tree structures to consume excessive resources.

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Create large data structures (lists/dicts with 100k+ elements)
2. Trigger locals() logging that involves these structures
3. Observe excessive memory usage and processing time during traversal
4. Notice that limits are only applied after full traversal completes

### 1.5 Best Practices for Fix
- Apply limits during traversal, not after
- Implement configurable iteration limits
- Add recursion depth tracking with limits
- Maintain backward compatibility
- Ensure minimal performance impact for normal-sized data

### 1.1-1.5 Problem Analysis

**Problem Summary**: When reading a grouped netCDF file that contains subgroups and has an unlimited dimension, the `cfdm.read()` function incorrectly reports the unlimited dimension size as 0 instead of its actual size (13 in the example).

**Technical Details**:
- **Method affected**: `cfdm.read_write.netcdf.NetCDFRead`
- **File type**: Grouped netCDF files with subgroups
- **Error manifestation**: Unlimited dimension shows size 0 instead of actual size
- **Root cause**: Dimension sizes are taken from flattened version of file, which loses unlimited dimension size information

**Steps to Reproduce**:
1. Obtain a grouped netCDF file with an unlimited dimension (like `cm4twc_dump_file.nc`)
2. Call `cfdm.read('filename.nc')[0]`
3. Observe incorrect dimension size (0 instead of actual size like 13)

**Best Practices for Fix**:
- Get dimension sizes from original grouped file instead of flattened version
- Maintain compatibility with non-grouped files
- Make minimal, targeted changes
- Ensure comprehensive testing

    33	Functionality
    34	=============
    35	
    36	The ``cfdm`` package implements the CF data model
    37	(https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-10-4619-2017) for its internal data
    38	structures and so is able to process any CF-compliant dataset. It is
    39	not strict about CF-compliance, however, so that partially conformant
    40	datasets may be ingested from existing datasets and written to new
    41	datasets. This is so that datasets which are partially conformant may
    42	nonetheless be modified in memory.
    43	
    44	The central element defined by the CF data model is the **field
    45	construct**, which corresponds to a CF-netCDF data variable with all
    46	of its metadata.
    47	
    48	A simple example of reading a field construct from a file and
    49	inspecting it:
    50	
    51	    >>> import cfdm
    52	    >>> f = cfdm.read('file.nc')
    53	    >>> f
    54	    [<Field: air_temperature(time(12), latitude(64), longitude(128)) K>]
    55	    >>> print(f[0])
    56	    Field: air_temperature (ncvar%tas)
    57	    ----------------------------------
    58	    Data            : air_temperature(time(12), latitude(64), longitude(128)) K
    59	    Cell methods    : time(12): mean (interval: 1.0 month)
    60	    Dimension coords: time(12) = [0450-11-16 00:00:00, ..., 0451-10-16 12:00:00] noleap
    61	                    : latitude(64) = [-87.8638, ..., 87.8638] degrees_north
    62	                    : longitude(128) = [0.0, ..., 357.1875] degrees_east
    63	                    : height(1) = [2.0] m
    64	
    65	The ``cfdm`` package can:
    66	
    67	* read field constructs from netCDF and CDL datasets,
    68	* create new field constructs in memory,
    69	* write field constructs to netCDF datasets on disk,
    70	* read, write, and create coordinates defined by geometry cells,
    71	* read and write netCDF4 string data-type variables,
    72	* read, write, and create netCDF and CDL datasets containing
    73	  hierarchical groups,
    74	* inspect field constructs,
    75	* test whether two field constructs are the same,
    76	* modify field construct metadata and data,
    77	* create subspaces of field constructs,
    78	* incorporate, and create, metadata stored in external files, and
    79	* read, write, and create data that have been compressed by convention
    80	  (i.e. ragged or gathered arrays), whilst presenting a view of the
    81	  data in its uncompressed form.
    82	
    83	Command line utility
    84	====================
    85	
    86	During installation the `cfdump` command line tool is also installed,
    87	which generates text descriptions of the field constructs contained in

3. In Python 2.7, this triggers infinite recursion

The issue is with **SQLGlot's DuckDB parser** failing to recognize the type specification `struct(a bigint)[]` in a CAST expression.

- **Error Message**: `ParseError: Expected TYPE after CAST. Line 1, Col: 38.`
- **Method**: `sg.parse_one()` with `read="duckdb"` parameter
- **Failing SQL**: `select cast([struct_pack(a := 1)] as struct(a bigint)[])`
- **Column Position**: 38 (right after "as" in the CAST expression)
- **Type Specification**: `struct(a bigint)[]` (array of structs)

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Import sqlglot library
2. Call `sg.parse_one("select cast([struct_pack(a := 1)] as struct(a bigint)[])", read="duckdb")`
3. Parser throws ParseError instead of successfully parsing the statement

### 1.5 Best Practices for Testing and Fixing
- Understand DuckDB's syntax for struct and array types
- Locate parser grammar rules for type specifications
- Ensure backward compatibility with existing type parsing

     7	You can easily [customize](#custom-dialects) the parser, [analyze](#metadata) queries, traverse expression trees, and programmatically [build](#build-and-modify-sql) SQL.
     8	
     9	Syntax [errors](#parser-errors) are highlighted and dialect incompatibilities can warn or raise depending on configurations. However, it should be noted that SQL validation is not SQLGlot’s goal, so some syntax errors may go unnoticed.
    10

    59	### Formatting and Transpiling
    60	
    61	Easily translate from one dialect to another. For example, date/time functions vary from dialects and can be hard to deal with:
    62	
    63	```python
    64	import sqlglot
    65	sqlglot.transpile("SELECT EPOCH_MS(1618088028295)", read="duckdb", write="hive")[0]
    66	```
    67	
    68	```sql
    69	'SELECT FROM_UNIXTIME(1618088028295 / 1000)'
    70	```
    71	
    72	SQLGlot can even translate custom time formats:
    73	
    74	```python
    75	import sqlglot
    76	sqlglot.transpile("SELECT STRFTIME(x, '%y-%-m-%S')", read="duckdb", write="hive")[0]
    77	```
    78	
    79	```sql
    80	"SELECT DATE_FORMAT(x, 'yy-M-ss')"
    81	```
    82	
    83	As another example, let's suppose that we want to read in a SQL query that contains a CTE and a cast to `REAL`, and then transpile it to Spark, which uses backticks for identifiers and `FLOAT` instead of `REAL`:
    84	
    85	```python
    86	import sqlglot
    87	
    88	sql = """WITH baz AS (SELECT a, c FROM foo WHERE a = 1) SELECT f.a, b.b, baz.c, CAST("b"."a" AS REAL) d FROM foo f JOIN bar b ON f.a = b.a LEFT JOIN baz ON f.a = baz.a"""
    89	print(sqlglot.transpile(sql, write="spark", identify=True, pretty=True)[0])
    90	```
    91	
    92	```sql
    93	WITH `baz` AS (
    94	  SELECT
    95	    `a`,
    96	    `c`
    97	  FROM `foo`
    98	  WHERE
    99	    `a` = 1
   100	)
   101	SELECT
   102	  `f`.`a`,
   103	  `b`.`b`,
   104	  `baz`.`c`,
   105	  CAST(`b`.`a` AS FLOAT) AS `d`
   106	FROM `foo` AS `f`
   107	JOIN `bar` AS `b`
   108	  ON `f`.`a` = `b`.`a`
   109	LEFT JOIN `baz`
   110	  ON `f`.`a` = `baz`.`a`
   111	```
   112	
   113	Comments are also preserved in a best-effort basis when transpiling SQL code:
   114	
   115	```python
   116	sql = """
   117	/* multi
   118	   line
   119	   comment
   120	*/
   121	SELECT
   122	  tbl.cola /* comment 1 */ + tbl.colb /* comment 2 */,
   123	  CAST(x AS INT), # comment 3
   124	  y               -- comment 4
   125	FROM
   126	  bar /* comment 5 */,
   127	  tbl #          comment 6
   128	"""
   129	
   130	print(sqlglot.transpile(sql, read='mysql', pretty=True)[0])
   131	```
   132	
   133	```sql
   134	/* multi
   135	   line
   136	   comment
   137	*/
   138	SELECT
   139	  tbl.cola /* comment 1 */ + tbl.colb /* comment 2 */,
   140	  CAST(x AS INT), /* comment 3 */
   141	  y /* comment 4 */
   142	FROM bar /* comment 5 */, tbl /*          comment 6 */
   143	```

   146	### Metadata
   147	
   148	You can explore SQL with expression helpers to do things like find columns and tables:
   149	
   150	```python
   151	from sqlglot import parse_one, exp
   152	
   153	# print all column references (a and b)
   154	for column in parse_one("SELECT a, b + 1 AS c FROM d").find_all(exp.Column):
   155	    print(column.alias_or_name)
   156	
   157	# find all projections in select statements (a and c)
   158	for select in parse_one("SELECT a, b + 1 AS c FROM d").find_all(exp.Select):
   159	    for projection in select.expressions:
   160	        print(projection.alias_or_name)
   161	
   162	# find all tables (x, y, z)
   163	for table in parse_one("SELECT * FROM x JOIN y JOIN z").find_all(exp.Table):
   164	    print(table.name)
   165	```
   166	
   167	### Parser Errors
   168	
   169	When the parser detects an error in the syntax, it raises a ParserError:
   170	
   171	```python
   172	import sqlglot
   173	sqlglot.transpile("SELECT foo( FROM bar")
   174	```
   175	
   176	```
   177	sqlglot.errors.ParseError: Expecting ). Line 1, Col: 13.
   178	  select foo( FROM bar
   179	              ~~~~
   180	```
   181	
   182	Structured syntax errors are accessible for programmatic use:
   183	
   184	```python
   185	import sqlglot
   186	try:
   187	    sqlglot.transpile("SELECT foo( FROM bar")
   188	except sqlglot.errors.ParseError as e:
   189	    print(e.errors)
   190	```
   191	
   192	```python
   193	[{
   194	  'description': 'Expecting )',
   195	  'line': 1,
   196	  'col': 13,
   197	  'start_context': 'SELECT foo( ',
   198	  'highlight': 'FROM',
   199	  'end_context': ' bar'
   200	}]
   201	```
   202	
   203	### Unsupported Errors
   204	
   205	Presto `APPROX_DISTINCT` supports the accuracy argument which is not supported in Hive:
   206	
   207	```python
   208	import sqlglot
   209	sqlglot.transpile("SELECT APPROX_DISTINCT(a, 0.1) FROM foo", read="presto", write="hive")
   210	```
   211	
   212	```sql
   213	APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT does not support accuracy
   214	'SELECT APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(a) FROM foo'
   215	```

   217	### Build and Modify SQL
   218	
   219	SQLGlot supports incrementally building sql expressions:
   220	
   221	```python
   222	from sqlglot import select, condition
   223	
   224	where = condition("x=1").and_("y=1")
   225	select("*").from_("y").where(where).sql()
   226	```
   227	
   228	```sql
   229	'SELECT * FROM y WHERE x = 1 AND y = 1'
   230	```
   231	
   232	You can also modify a parsed tree:
   233	
   234	```python
   235	from sqlglot import parse_one
   236	parse_one("SELECT x FROM y").from_("z").sql()
   237	```
   238	
   239	```sql
   240	'SELECT x FROM y, z'
   241	```
   242	
   243	There is also a way to recursively transform the parsed tree by applying a mapping function to each tree node:
   244	
   245	```python
   246	from sqlglot import exp, parse_one
   247	
   248	expression_tree = parse_one("SELECT a FROM x")
   249	
   250	def transformer(node):
   251	    if isinstance(node, exp.Column) and node.name == "a":
   252	        return parse_one("FUN(a)")
   253	    return node
   254	
   255	transformed_tree = expression_tree.transform(transformer)
   256	transformed_tree.sql()
   257	```
   258	
   259	```sql
   260	'SELECT FUN(a) FROM x'
   261	```

   263	### SQL Optimizer
   264	
   265	SQLGlot can rewrite queries into an "optimized" form. It performs a variety of [techniques](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/main/sqlglot/optimizer/optimizer.py) to create a new canonical AST. This AST can be used to standardize queries or provide the foundations for implementing an actual engine. For example:
   266	
   267	```python
   268	import sqlglot
   269	from sqlglot.optimizer import optimize
   270	
   271	print(
   272	    optimize(
   273	        sqlglot.parse_one("""
   274	            SELECT A OR (B OR (C AND D))
   275	            FROM x
   276	            WHERE Z = date '2021-01-01' + INTERVAL '1' month OR 1 = 0
   277	        """),
   278	        schema={"x": {"A": "INT", "B": "INT", "C": "INT", "D": "INT", "Z": "STRING"}}
   279	    ).sql(pretty=True)
   280	)
   281	```
   282	
   283	```sql
   284	SELECT
   285	  (
   286	    "x"."a" OR "x"."b" OR "x"."c"
   287	  ) AND (
   288	    "x"."a" OR "x"."b" OR "x"."d"
   289	  ) AS "_col_0"
   290	FROM "x" AS "x"
   291	WHERE
   292	  CAST("x"."z" AS DATE) = CAST('2021-02-01' AS DATE)
   293	```
   294	
   295	### AST Introspection
   296	
   297	You can see the AST version of the sql by calling `repr`:
   298	
   299	```python
   300	from sqlglot import parse_one
   301	print(repr(parse_one("SELECT a + 1 AS z")))
   302	```
   303	
   304	```python
   305	(SELECT expressions:
   306	  (ALIAS this:
   307	    (ADD this:
   308	      (COLUMN this:
   309	        (IDENTIFIER this: a, quoted: False)), expression:
   310	      (LITERAL this: 1, is_string: False)), alias:
   311	    (IDENTIFIER this: z, quoted: False)))
   312	```
   313	
   314	### AST Diff
   315	
   316	SQLGlot can calculate the difference between two expressions and output changes in a form of a sequence of actions needed to transform a source expression into a target one:
   317	
   318	```python
   319	from sqlglot import diff, parse_one
   320	diff(parse_one("SELECT a + b, c, d"), parse_one("SELECT c, a - b, d"))
   321	```
   322	
   323	```python
   324	[
   325	  Remove(expression=(ADD this:
   326	    (COLUMN this:
   327	      (IDENTIFIER this: a, quoted: False)), expression:
   328	    (COLUMN this:
   329	      (IDENTIFIER this: b, quoted: False)))),
   330	  Insert(expression=(SUB this:
   331	    (COLUMN this:
   332	      (IDENTIFIER this: a, quoted: False)), expression:
   333	    (COLUMN this:
   334	      (IDENTIFIER this: b, quoted: False)))),
   335	  Move(expression=(COLUMN this:
   336	    (IDENTIFIER this: c, quoted: False))),
   337	  Keep(source=(IDENTIFIER this: b, quoted: False), target=(IDENTIFIER this: b, quoted: False)),
   338	  ...
   339	]
   340	```
   341	
   342	See also: [Semantic Diff for SQL](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/main/posts/sql_diff.md).

   344	### Custom Dialects
   345	
   346	[Dialects](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/tree/main/sqlglot/dialects) can be added by subclassing `Dialect`:
   347	
   348	```python
   349	from sqlglot import exp
   350	from sqlglot.dialects.dialect import Dialect
   351	from sqlglot.generator import Generator
   352	from sqlglot.tokens import Tokenizer, TokenType
   353	
   354	
   355	class Custom(Dialect):
   356	    class Tokenizer(Tokenizer):
   357	        QUOTES = ["'", '"']
   358	        IDENTIFIERS = ["`"]
   359	
   360	        KEYWORDS = {
   361	            **Tokenizer.KEYWORDS,
   362	            "INT64": TokenType.BIGINT,
   363	            "FLOAT64": TokenType.DOUBLE,
   364	        }
   365	
   366	    class Generator(Generator):
   367	        TRANSFORMS = {exp.Array: lambda self, e: f"[{self.expressions(e)}]"}
   368	
   369	        TYPE_MAPPING = {
   370	            exp.DataType.Type.TINYINT: "INT64",
   371	            exp.DataType.Type.SMALLINT: "INT64",
   372	            exp.DataType.Type.INT: "INT64",
   373	            exp.DataType.Type.BIGINT: "INT64",
   374	            exp.DataType.Type.DECIMAL: "NUMERIC",
   375	            exp.DataType.Type.FLOAT: "FLOAT64",
   376	            exp.DataType.Type.DOUBLE: "FLOAT64",
   377	            exp.DataType.Type.BOOLEAN: "BOOL",
   378	            exp.DataType.Type.TEXT: "STRING",
   379	        }
   380	
   381	print(Dialect["custom"])
   382	```
   383	
   384	```
   385	<class '__main__.Custom'>
   386	```

   388	### SQL Execution
   389	
   390	One can even interpret SQL queries using SQLGlot, where the tables are represented as Python dictionaries. Although the engine is not very fast (it's not supposed to be) and is in a relatively early stage of development, it can be useful for unit testing and running SQL natively across Python objects. Additionally, the foundation can be easily integrated with fast compute kernels (arrow, pandas). Below is an example showcasing the execution of a SELECT expression that involves aggregations and JOINs:
   391	
   392	```python
   393	from sqlglot.executor import execute
   394	
   395	tables = {
   396	    "sushi": [
   397	        {"id": 1, "price": 1.0},
   398	        {"id": 2, "price": 2.0},
   399	        {"id": 3, "price": 3.0},
   400	    ],
   401	    "order_items": [
   402	        {"sushi_id": 1, "order_id": 1},
   403	        {"sushi_id": 1, "order_id": 1},
   404	        {"sushi_id": 2, "order_id": 1},
   405	        {"sushi_id": 3, "order_id": 2},
   406	    ],
   407	    "orders": [
   408	        {"id": 1, "user_id": 1},
   409	        {"id": 2, "user_id": 2},
   410	    ],
   411	}
   412	
   413	execute(
   414	    """
   415	    SELECT
   416	      o.user_id,
   417	      SUM(s.price) AS price
   418	    FROM orders o
   419	    JOIN order_items i
   420	      ON o.id = i.order_id
   421	    JOIN sushi s
   422	      ON i.sushi_id = s.id
   423	    GROUP BY o.user_id
   424	    """,
   425	    tables=tables
   426	)
   427	```
   428	
   429	```python
   430	user_id price
   431	      1   4.0
   432	      2   3.0
   433	```
   434	
   435	See also: [Writing a Python SQL engine from scratch](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/main/posts/python_sql_engine.md).

- `spanner/dbapi/connection.py` line 60 in `commit` method

**Problem Explanation:**
The Spanner client library is reusing sequence numbers (seqno) for different requests within the same transaction or session. The Spanner backend detects this duplication and rejects subsequent requests with the same seqno but different content, causing test failures during Django fixture setup.

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Run Django tests that involve database operations
2. During test setup, Django tries to create fixtures/users
3. Multiple SQL statements are executed within transactions
4. Sequence numbers get reused incorrectly, triggering the error

### 1.5 Best Practices for Fix
- Ensure sequence numbers are unique within transaction sessions
- Maintain proper transaction state management
- Make minimal changes to avoid breaking existing functionality
- Focus on the DBAPI layer where the error originates

- **Error Message**: `ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (5,) (3,)`
- **Method Names**: `QNGOptimizer.step()`, `metric_tensor()`, `apply_grad()`
- **File Location**: `/pennylane/optimize/qng.py` line 277
- **Variables**: `data` (non-trainable), `params` (trainable)
- **Stack Trace**: Error occurs in `x_new_flat = x_flat - self.stepsize * pnp.linalg.solve(self.metric_tensor, grad_flat)`

### 1.3 Clear Problem Statement

The QNGOptimizer fails when optimizing circuits with multiple arguments because:
1. The metric tensor calculation and gradient calculation don't align properly when dealing with multiple argument arrays
2. The flattening/unflattening process treats all arguments as a single flat array, but the metric tensor and gradient have different dimensional expectations
3. Specifically, when data (shape 2) and params (shape 3) are combined, the total is 5 elements, but only the trainable params (3 elements) contribute to the gradient

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a QNode with multiple arguments (data and params)
2. Set data as non-trainable (`requires_grad=False`) and params as trainable (`requires_grad=True`)
3. Create a QNGOptimizer instance
4. Create a metric tensor function using `qml.metric_tensor(circuit)`
5. Call `optimizer.step(cost_function, data, params, metric_tensor_fn=mt_fn)`
6. Observe the shape mismatch error

### 1.5 Best Practices for Testing and Fixing

- Understand how metric_tensor handles multiple arguments internally
- Ensure backward compatibility with single-argument circuits
- Test with various combinations of trainable/non-trainable arguments
- Consider documenting limitations if a complete fix isn't feasible

    # If x is even, increment it

    # If x is odd, negate it

    18	|TatSu|
    19	=======
    20	
    21	|TatSu| (the successor to Grako_) is a tool that takes grammars in a
    22	variation of `EBNF`_ as input, and outputs `memoizing`_ (`Packrat`_)
    23	`PEG`_ parsers in `Python`_.
    24	
    25	|TatSu| can compile a grammar stored in a string into a
    26	``tatsu.grammars.Grammar`` object that can be used to parse any given
    27	input, much like the `re`_ module does with regular expressions, or it can generate a Python_ module that implements the parser.
    28	
    29	|TatSu| fully supports `left-recursive`_  rules in PEG_ grammars using the algorithm_ by *Laurent* and *Mens*. The generated AST_ has the expected left associativity.
    30	
    31	.. _algorithm: http://norswap.com/pubs/sle2016.pdf
    32	
    33	Installation
    34	------------
    35	
    36	.. code:: bash
    37	
    38	    $ pip install TatSu
    39	
    40	
    41	Using the Tool
    42	--------------
    43	
    44	|TatSu| can be used as a library, much like `Python`_'s ``re``, by embedding grammars as strings and generating grammar models instead of generating Python_ code.
    45	
    46	-   ``tatsu.compile(grammar, name=None, **kwargs)``
    47	
    48	    Compiles the grammar and generates a *model* that can subsequently be used for parsing input with.
    49	
    50	-   ``tatsu.parse(grammar, input, **kwargs)``
    51	
    52	    Compiles the grammar and parses the given input producing an AST_ as result. The result is equivalent to calling::
    53	
    54	        model = compile(grammar)
    55	        ast = model.parse(input)
    56	
    57	    Compiled grammars are cached for efficiency.
    58	
    59	-   ``tatsu.to_python_sourcecode(grammar, name=None, filename=None, **kwargs)``
    60	
    61	    Compiles the grammar to the `Python`_ sourcecode that implements the parser.

_Issue [JP-3429](https://jira.stsci.edu/browse/JP-3429) was created on JIRA by [Melanie Clarke](https://jira.stsci.edu/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=mclarke):_

In particular, the combine_fast_slow function needs to be updated to take an error array as input and interpolate it onto the wavelengths for the observation.  The interpolated error should then be added in quadrature to any error from other components.

Two implementation notes:

1. Both zero and NaN are possible values for all flat error arrays, 2D and 1D.  The S and D flats will not have error arrays for their 1D components, so these values will default to NaN; their 2D error components will be set to zero, since all flat errors are accounted for in the F-flat instead. When combining flat error values, NaN values should be ignored and zero values should be treated as valid numbers.  

2. The 1D flat vector in the combine_fast_slow algorithm is interpolated with a 3-point Gaussian integration.  A rigorous error propagation through that step should take into account cross-correlations between the pixels that are weighted and summed together, but we don't recommend that.  The flat errors are not likely to be known to enough precision to justify the complexity.  Instead, we recommend interpolating the error vector onto the wavelengths with a simple linear interpolation, e.g.:
  error_value = np.interp(wavelengths, tab_wl, tab_flat_error, left=np.nan, right=np.nan)

     3	ufo2ft
     4	======
     5	
     6	ufo2ft ("UFO to FontTools") is a fork of
     7	`ufo2fdk <https://github.com/typesupply/ufo2fdk>`__ whose goal is to
     8	generate OpenType font binaries from UFOs without the FDK dependency.
     9	
    10	The library provides two functions, ``compileOTF`` and ``compileTTF``,
    11	which work exactly the same way:
    12	
    13	.. code:: python
    14	
    15	    from defcon import Font
    16	    from ufo2ft import compileOTF
    17	    ufo = Font('MyFont-Regular.ufo')
    18	    otf = compileOTF(ufo)
    19	    otf.save('MyFont-Regular.otf')
    20	
    21	In most cases, the behavior of ufo2ft should match that of ufo2fdk,
    22	whose documentation is retained below (and hopefully is still accurate).
    23	
    24	Naming Data
    25	~~~~~~~~~~~
    26	
    27	As with any OpenType compiler, you have to set the font naming data to a
    28	particular standard for your naming to be set correctly. In ufo2fdk, you
    29	can get away with setting *two* naming attributes in your font.info
    30	object for simple fonts:
    31	
    32	-  familyName: The name for your family. For example, "My Garamond".
    33	-  styleName: The style name for this particular font. For example,
    34	   "Display Light Italic"
    35	
    36	ufo2fdk will create all of the other naming data based on thse two
    37	fields. If you want to use the fully automatic naming system, all of the
    38	other name attributes should be set to ``None`` in your font. However,
    39	if you want to override the automated system at any level, you can
    40	specify particular naming attributes and ufo2fdk will honor your
    41	settings. You don't have to set *all* of the attributes, just the ones
    42	you don't want to be automated. For example, in the family "My Garamond"
    43	you have eight weights. It would be nice to style map the italics to the
    44	romans for each weight. To do this, in the individual romans and
    45	italics, you need to set the style mapping data. This is done through
    46	the ``styleMapFamilyName`` and ``styleMapStyleName`` attributes. In each
    47	of your roman and italic pairs you would do this:
    48	
    49	**My Garamond-Light.ufo**
    50	
    51	-  familyName = "My Garamond"
    52	-  styleName = "Light"
    53	-  styleMapFamilyName = "My Garamond Display Light"
    54	-  styleMapStyleName = "regular"
    55	
    56	**My Garamond-Light Italic.ufo**
    57	
    58	-  familyName = "My Garamond"
    59	-  styleName = "Display Light Italic"
    60	-  styleMapFamilyName = "My Garamond Display Light"
    61	-  styleMapStyleName = "italic"
    62	
    63	**My Garamond-Book.ufo**
    64	
    65	-  familyName = "My Garamond"
    66	-  styleName = "Book"
    67	-  styleMapFamilyName = "My Garamond Display Book"
    68	-  styleMapStyleName = "regular"
    69	
    70	**My Garamond-Book Italic.ufo**
    71	
    72	-  familyName = "My Garamond"
    73	-  styleName = "Display Book Italic"
    74	-  styleMapFamilyName = "My Garamond Display Book"
    75	-  styleMapStyleName = "italic"
    76	
    77	**etc.**
    78	
    79	Additionally, if you have defined any naming data, or any data for that
    80	matter, in table definitions within your font's features that data will
    81	be honored.
    82	
    83	
    84	Feature generation
    85	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    86	
    87	If your font's features do not contain kerning/mark/mkmk features,
    88	ufo2ft will create them based on your font's kerning/anchor data.
    89	
    90	In addition to
    91	`Adobe OpenType feature files <http://www.adobe.com/devnet/opentype/afdko/topic_feature_file_syntax.html>`__,
    92	ufo2ft also supports the
    93	`MTI/Monotype format <http://monotype.github.io/OpenType_Table_Source/otl_source.html>`__.
    94	For example, a GPOS table in this format would be stored within the UFO at
    95	``data/com.github.googlei18n.ufo2ft.mtiFeatures/GPOS.mti``.
    96	
    97

    99	~~~~~~~~~
   100	
   101	Most of the fallbacks have static values. To see what is set for these,
   102	look at ``fontInfoData.py`` in the source code.
   103	
   104	In some cases, the fallback values are dynamically generated from other
   105	data in the info object. These are handled internally with functions.
   106	
   107	Merging TTX
   108	~~~~~~~~~~~
   109	
   110	If the UFO data directory has a ``com.github.fonttools.ttx`` folder with TTX
   111	files ending with ``.ttx``, these will be merged in the generated font.
   112	The index TTX (generated when using using ``ttx -s``) is not required.

   124	Color fonts
   125	~~~~~~~~~~~
   126	
   127	ufo2ft supports building ``COLR`` and ``CPAL`` tables.
   128	
   129	If there is ``com.github.googlei18n.ufo2ft.colorPalettes`` key in font lib, and
   130	``com.github.googlei18n.ufo2ft.colorLayerMapping`` key in the font or
   131	in any of the glyphs lib, then ufo2ft will build ``CPAL`` table from the color
   132	palettes, and ``COLR`` table from the color layers.
   133	
   134	``colorPalettes`` is a array of palettes, each palette is a array of colors and
   135	each color is a array of floats representing RGBA colors. For example:
   136	
   137	.. code:: xml
   138	
   139	    <key>com.github.googlei18n.ufo2ft.colorPalettes</key>
   140	    <array>
   141	      <array>
   142	        <array>
   143	          <real>0.26</real>
   144	          <real>0.0</real>
   145	          <real>0.23</real>
   146	          <real>1.0</real>
   147	        </array>

   150	          <real>0.73</real>
   151	          <real>0.28</real>
   152	          <real>1.0</real>
   153	        </array>
   154	      </array>
   155	    </array>
   156	
   157	
   158	``colorLayerMapping`` is a array of color layers, each color layer is a array of
   159	layer name and palette color index. It is a per-glyph key, but if present in

   165	      <array>
   166	        <array>
   167	          <string>color.1</string>
   168	          <integer>1</integer>
   169	        </array>
   170	        <array>
   171	          <string>color.2</string>
   172	          <integer>0</integer>
   173	        </array>
   174	      </array>
   175	
   176	With these this key present, ufo2ft will copy the color layers into individual
   177	glyphs and setup ``COLR`` table.
   178

   189	      <array>

   203	          <integer>2</integer>

    * Sharing variables across different envs (base, local etc)

# Possible Implementation

To use globals, in your project -
* Update `settings.py`
```python
CONFIG_LOADER_ARGS = {
    "globals_pattern": "*globals.yml"
}
```
* Add `globals.yml` to `conf/base/` or `conf/local`
* To use global values in `parameters.yml` or `catalog.yml` 
`globals.yml`
```yaml
datasets: 
    csv: pandas.CSVDataSet

test_size: 0.3
```
`catalog.yml`
```yaml
reviews:
  type: ${globals:"datasets.csv"}
  filepath: <path_to_file>
```
`parameters.yml`
```yaml
model_options:
    test_size: ${globals:"test_size"}
```
Here "`globals`" is a custom resolver - https://omegaconf.readthedocs.io/en/latest/custom_resolvers.html#id9


> **Q: Configurable `globals_pattern`?**
> A: Allow users to pass `globals_pattern` through `settings.py` but have it be `globals_pattern: {"*globals.yml"}` by default.
> 
> **Q: Where would `globals.yml` go?**
> A: The `globals.yml` files would stay within `conf/base/` and `conf/local/` instead of a top level `conf/globals.yml`. The common keys in `local/globals.yml` will overwrite the ones in `base/globals.yml`
> ```
> conf/
>   |_ base/
>     |_ globals.yml
>     |_ catalog.yml
>   |_ local/
>     |_ globals.yml
>     |_ catalog.yml
> ```
> 
> **Q: Soft or hard merge common keys?**
> A: Overwrite keys from `base/globals.yml` with keys from `local/globals.yml` for now but allow soft-merging in Kedro 0.19
> 
> **Q: Allow `globals_dict` like `TemplatedConfigLoader`?`**
> A: No, this use case for dynamically providing global values can be solved using "custom resolvers"
> 
> _Originally posted by @ankatiyar in https://github.com/kedro-org/kedro/issues/2175#issuecomment-1634269590_

### 1.1-1.3 Problem Analysis

The issue describes a problem with the Spanner client library where:
- **Error Message**: "Received unexpected EOS on DATA frame from server"
- **Context**: Long-lived PDML (Partitioned DML) transactions lasting 30+ minutes with large data changes
- **Technical Details**: gRPC connection termination during streaming operations
- **Method/Feature**: PDML (Partitioned Data Manipulation Language) transactions

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Execute a large PDML operation that takes 30+ minutes
2. Wait for gRPC connection to terminate with "Received unexpected EOS on DATA frame from server"
3. Observe that the transaction fails instead of retrying

### 1.5 Best Practices
- Implement retry logic with resume tokens when available
- Fall back to restarting from scratch if resume tokens aren't available
- Continue retrying until success or hard timeout
- Follow patterns from existing Java implementation
- Make minimal, focused changes

     6	A [**Poetry**](https://python-poetry.org/) plugin for Poetry mono repositories, that will replace path dependencies with named dependency specifications.
     7	
     8	A mono repository contains multiple Python packages, which can depend on each other.
     9	These are typically path dependencies with the `develop = true` attribute.
    10	This allows for easy development and local running.
    11	However, when the packages are published to a PyPi repo, these dependencies should be named dependencies.
    12	By publishing the packages with named dependencies, one can easily install the packages and their dependencies.
    13	
    14	This plugin will replace path dependencies (`name @ path`) with named dependency specifications (`name ~= version`).
    15	By default, this is done when building artifacts ([`poetry build`](https://python-poetry.org/docs/main/cli/#build)) and exporting the locked dependency list ([`poetry export`](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry-plugin-export)).
    16	The plugin can however be configured to modify any other command registered by Poetry or other plugins.
    17	
    18	## An example using build and export
    19	
    20	Suppose you have a single folder with 2 Python packages, where one (`app-b`) depends on the other (`lib-a`).
    21	
    22	The used library has the following in its Poetry section:
    23	
    24	```toml
    25	# repo/A/pyproject.toml
    26	[tool.poetry]
    27	name = "lib-a"
    28	version = "0.0.1"
    29	```
    30	
    31	The application package depends on the previous library as follows:
    32	
    33	```toml
    34	# repo/B/pyproject.toml
    35	[tool.poetry]
    36	name = "app-B"
    37	
    38	[tool.poetry.dependencies]
    39	library-a = {path = "../A", develop=true}
    40	```
    41	
    42	### Poetry build
    43	
    44	By default, building the above project with Poetry (`poetry build`), will result in a build artifact (`tar.gz`/`whl`) containing a path dependency in its metadata similar to:
    45	
    46	```
    47	Requires-Dist: lib-a @ file:///your/local/checkout/project/root/lib-a
    48	```
    49	
    50	This prevents sharing the build and reusing the build artifact on other systems, as it expects to find `lib-a` at that specific path.
    51	
    52	Using this Mono-Repo-Deps plugin, the Poetry build will result in the following dependency:
    53	
    54	```
    55	Requires-Dist: lib-a (>=0.0.1,<0.1.0)
    56	```
    57	
    58	### Poetry export
    59	
    60	By default, exporting the full dependency list (`poetry export`) results in a dependency list (`requirements.txt`) that also contain path dedendencies with full paths:
    61	
    62	```
    63	lib-a @ file:///your/local/checkout/project/root/lib-a
    64	```
    65	
    66	Again, by using this Mono-Repo-Deps plugin, these will become:
    67	
    68	```
    69	lib-a==0.1.0
    70	```
    71	
    72	## Installation
    73	
    74	You can install the plugin as explained in the [Poetry documentation about plugin usage](https://python-poetry.org/docs/main/plugins/#using-plugins).
    75	
    76	Which can be summarized as:
    77	
    78	If you used PipX to install Poetry:
    79	
    80	```shell
    81	pipx inject poetry poetry-plugin-mono-repo-deps
    82	```
    83	
    84	If you used Pip to install Poetry:
    85	
    86	```shell
    87	pip install poetry-plugin-mono-repo-deps
    88	```
    89	
    90	On non-Windows devices, you can also use Poetry's `self add` which will also validate compatibility:
    91	
    92	```shell
    93	poetry self add poetry-plugin-mono-repo-deps
    94	```
    95	
    96	## Usage:
    97	
    98	As plugins are installed systemwide, **this plugin is by default disabled** to not unintentionally modify the existing behavior of Poetry.
    99	
   100	Enable the plugin by adding the following (empty) section to your `pyproject.toml`:
   101	
   102	```toml
   103	# repo/B/pyproject.toml
   104	[tool.poetry-monorepo.deps]
   105	```
   106	
   107	This is equivalent to adding the following default settings:
   108	
   109	```toml
   110	[tool.poetry-monorepo.deps]
   111	enabled = true
   112	commands = ["build", "export"]
   113	constraint = "~="
   114	source_types = ["file", "directory"]
   115	only_develop = false
   116	```
   117	
   118	Possible alternative values can be found in the following section:
   119	
   120	## Configuration:
   121	
   122	### `enabled`
   123	
   124	**Type**: `boolean`
   125	
   126	**Default**: `true`
   127	
   128	**Allowed values**: `true`, `false`
   129	
   130	Whether the plugin should be activated for commands on this project.
   131	
   132	### `commands`
   133	
   134	**Type**: `List[string]`
   135	
   136	**Default**: `["build", "export"]`
   137	
   138	**Allowed values**: Any CLI command registered with Poetry (could also be provided by other plugins).
   139	
   140	The intercepted poetry commands.
   141	The plugin will intercept the command and update the internal representation of dependencies, changing the path dependencies to named dependency specifications.
   142	
   143	### `constraint`
   144	
   145	**Type**: `string`
   146	
   147	**Default**: `~=`
   148	
   149	**Allowed values**: `==`, `>=` , `~=` , `^` (All [valid Poetry version constraints](https://python-poetry.org/docs/dependency-specification/)).
   150	
   151	The version constraint that is applied to the current version of the dependency.
   152	
   153	For example, when the dependency has version `0.0.1`, and the default constraint string `~=` is used, it will result in a named dependency with version `>=0.1.0, <0.1.0`.
   154	
   155	### `source_types`
   156	
   157	**Type**: `List[string]`
   158	
   159	**Default**: `["file", "directory"]` (local Path dependencies)
   160	
   161	**Allowed values**: `["file", "directory", "url", "git"]`. (Any `source_type` attribute of Poetry's internal Dependency object, which includes the lowercase VCS identifier, like `git`).
   162	
   163	The type of dependencies that should be replaced with their named version specification.
   164	
   165	### `only_develop`
   166	
   167	**Type**: `boolean`
   168	
   169	**Default**: `false`
   170	
   171	Enable to only replace `develop` dependencies, which, as currently implemented in Poetry, are only `directory` [Path dependencies](https://python-poetry.org/docs/main/dependency-specification/#path-dependencies).
   172	
   173	This filter is **only applied to directory path** dependencies, as only those can have the `develop` mark.
   174	
   175	If you configure `source_types` to be any Path dependency (ie. `file` or `directory`), all file path dependencies will be translated, while only the directory dependencies annotated with `develop = true` will be translated.
   176	
   177	## Caveats
   178	
   179	Currently, the plugin has only been verified to work with the `poetry build` and `poetry export` commands.
   180	Though theoretically it should work with any other (plugin's) command, your mileage may vary.
   181	
   182	## How it works
   183	
   184	If enabled, this plugin registers itself to run before specific commands.
   185	When these commands are run, it will modify the internal lock file representation that Poetry uses, replacing the path dependency objects with regular dependencies.
   186	
   187	The idea came from the [Python Poetry Monorepo without Limitations](https://gerben-oostra.medium.com/python-poetry-mono-repo-without-limitations-dd63b47dc6b8) blog post on Medium, which describes how a simple script can modify the `pyproject.toml` before a build step, resulting in named dependencies in the build artifacts.
   188	This plugin only temporarily modifies the structure, in memory, just for the command you run it on.
   189	
   190	## Contributing
   191	
   192	We recommend using PyEnv to select the right Python version:
   193	
   194	```console
   195	pyenv local && poetry env use $(which python)
   196	make venv
   197	```
   198	
   199	We use [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/), which most recent version requires Python >=3.9, while this project aims to work on Python >=3.8.
   200	Therefore install pre-commit on your system yourself (using Homebrew / PipX)
   201	
   202	Tests can be run with `make test`, linting with `make lint`
